rows.stem: The next term of the A.P. : \(\sqrt{7}, \sqrt{28}, \sqrt{63}\) is :
rows.solution:
\(\sqrt{28} = 2\sqrt{7}\) and \(\sqrt{63} = 3\sqrt{7}\), so the A.P. is \(\sqrt{7}, 2\sqrt{7}, 3\sqrt{7}, \ldots\) with common difference \(\sqrt{7}\).

The next term is \(4\sqrt{7} = \sqrt{16 \times 7} = \sqrt{112}\), which is option (D) \(\sqrt{112}\).

\(\sec^2\theta - 1 = \tan^2\theta\) and \(\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta - 1 = \cot^2\theta\).

So the product is \(\tan^2\theta \cot^2\theta = 1\), since \(\tan\theta \cot\theta = 1\). This is option (B) \(1\).

rows.stem:
For the following distribution :

| Marks Below | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Number of Students | 3 | 12 | 27 | 57 | 75 | 80 |

The modal class is :
rows.solution:
The table is cumulative ("less than"), so subtract to get the frequency of each class:

0-10: 3, 10-20: \(12 - 3 = 9\), 20-30: \(27 - 12 = 15\), 30-40: \(57 - 27 = 30\), 40-50: \(75 - 57 = 18\), 50-60: \(80 - 75 = 5\).

The highest frequency is 30, so the modal class is 30-40, which is option (C) 30-40.

rows.stem: In the given figure, PT is a tangent at T to the circle with centre O. If \(\angle TPO = 25^\circ\), then \(x\) is equal to :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - x is defined only in the drawing: it is the angle at O between OP and the diameter through T, on the side away from T (TO produced meets the circle below P's line). Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
The radius OT is perpendicular to the tangent PT, so \(\angle PTO = 90^\circ\).

In triangle PTO, \(\angle TOP = 180^\circ - 90^\circ - 25^\circ = 65^\circ\).

In the figure, x is the angle at O between OP and the diameter through T, on the far side from T, so x and \(\angle TOP\) form a linear pair: \(x = 180^\circ - 65^\circ = 115^\circ\), which is option (D) \(115^\circ\).

rows.stem: In the given figure, \(PQ \parallel AC\). If BP = 4 cm, AP = 2.4 cm and BQ = 5 cm, then length of BC is :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - that P lies on AB and Q on BC (triangle ABC with PQ drawn parallel to AC) is shown only in the drawing; the stem never names the triangle. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
In triangle ABC, P lies on AB and Q on BC, with \(PQ \parallel AC\). So \(\Delta BPQ \sim \Delta BAC\) (AA), and \(\dfrac{BP}{BA} = \dfrac{BQ}{BC}\).

\(BA = BP + PA = 4 + 2.4 = 6.4\) cm, so \(\dfrac{4}{6.4} = \dfrac{5}{BC}\) and \(BC = \dfrac{5 \times 6.4}{4} = 8\) cm.

This is option (A) \(8\) cm.

rows.stem: The points \((-4, 0)\), \((4, 0)\) and \((0, 3)\) are the vertices of a :
rows.solution:
Let the points be \(P(-4, 0)\), \(Q(4, 0)\) and \(R(0, 3)\).

\(PQ = 8\), \(PR = \sqrt{16 + 9} = 5\), \(QR = \sqrt{16 + 9} = 5\).

Two sides are equal, and \(PR^2 + QR^2 = 50 \neq 64 = PQ^2\), so the triangle is isosceles and not right-angled. This is option (B) isosceles triangle.

rows.stem: If \(\sin\theta - \cos\theta = 0\), then find the value of \(\sin^4\theta + \cos^4\theta\).
rows.solution:
\(\sin\theta - \cos\theta = 0\) gives \(\sin\theta = \cos\theta\), so \(\tan\theta = 1\) and \(\theta = 45^\circ\).

\(\sin^4 45^\circ + \cos^4 45^\circ = \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^4 + \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^4 = \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}\).

(Without finding \(\theta\): \(\sin^2\theta = \cos^2\theta\) and the two add up to 1, so each is \(\dfrac{1}{2}\), and the sum of their squares is \(\dfrac{1}{2}\).)

rows.subtopic: Zeroes and Coefficients of a Quadratic Polynomial
rows.stem: Find the value of 'p' for which one root of the quadratic equation \(px^2 - 14x + 8 = 0\) is 6 times the other.
rows.solution:
Let the roots be \(\alpha\) and \(6\alpha\).

Sum of the roots: \(\alpha + 6\alpha = \dfrac{14}{p}\), so \(7\alpha = \dfrac{14}{p}\) and \(\alpha = \dfrac{2}{p}\).

Product of the roots: \(\alpha \cdot 6\alpha = \dfrac{8}{p}\), so \(6\alpha^2 = \dfrac{8}{p}\).

Substituting \(\alpha = \dfrac{2}{p}\): \(6 \times \dfrac{4}{p^2} = \dfrac{8}{p}\), so \(24 = 8p\) and \(p = 3\).

Check: \(3x^2 - 14x + 8 = (3x - 2)(x - 4)\), with roots \(\dfrac{2}{3}\) and 4, and \(4 = 6 \times \dfrac{2}{3}\).

rows.subtopic: Number of Tangents from an External Point
rows.stem: From an external point, two tangents are drawn to a circle. Prove that the line joining the external point to the centre of the circle bisects the angle between the two tangents.
rows.solution:
Given: PA and PB are tangents drawn from an external point P to a circle with centre O, touching it at A and B.

To prove: OP bisects \(\angle APB\), that is \(\angle OPA = \angle OPB\).

Construction: join OA and OB.

Proof: in triangles OAP and OBP,

\(OA = OB\) (radii of the same circle),

\(OP = OP\) (common),

\(\angle OAP = \angle OBP = 90^\circ\) (the radius is perpendicular to the tangent at the point of contact).

So \(\Delta OAP \cong \Delta OBP\) (RHS congruence), and \(\angle OPA = \angle OPB\) (CPCT).

So the line joining the external point to the centre bisects the angle between the two tangents.

rows.stem: How many terms are there in A.P. whose first and fifth term are \(-14\) and 2, respectively and the last term is 62.
In a \(\Delta PQR\), N is a point on PR, such that \(QN \perp PR\). If \(PN \times NR = QN^2\), prove that \(\angle PQR = 90^\circ\).
rows.solution:
Let \(\angle 1 = \angle PQN\) and \(\angle 2 = \angle NQR\), so that \(\angle PQR = \angle 1 + \angle 2\).

\(PN \times NR = QN^2\) gives \(\dfrac{PN}{QN} = \dfrac{QN}{NR}\).

In triangles PNQ and QNR: \(\dfrac{PN}{QN} = \dfrac{QN}{NR}\), and \(\angle PNQ = \angle QNR = 90^\circ\) (since \(QN \perp PR\)).

So \(\Delta PNQ \sim \Delta QNR\) (SAS similarity), with P matching Q, N matching N and Q matching R.

Their corresponding angles are equal: \(\angle NPQ = \angle NQR\), that is \(\angle P = \angle 2\), and \(\angle PQN = \angle QRN\), that is \(\angle 1 = \angle R\).

Adding, \(\angle 1 + \angle 2 = \angle R + \angle P\), so \(\angle PQR = \angle P + \angle R\).

In triangle PQR, \(\angle P + \angle PQR + \angle R = 180^\circ\), so \(2\angle PQR = 180^\circ\) and \(\angle PQR = 90^\circ\).

rows.stem: In the given figure, \(\Delta ABC\) and \(\Delta DBC\) are on the same base BC. If AD intersects BC at O, prove that \(\dfrac{\text{ar}(\Delta ABC)}{\text{ar}(\Delta DBC)} = \dfrac{AO}{DO}\)
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - quadrilateral ABDC with A above and D below the base BC, and AD crossing BC at O; the stem states everything the proof needs. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
Draw \(AL \perp BC\) and \(DM \perp BC\), with L and M on BC.

In triangles AOL and DOM:

\(\angle AOL = \angle DOM\) (vertically opposite angles), and \(\angle ALO = \angle DMO = 90^\circ\).

So \(\Delta AOL \sim \Delta DOM\) (AA similarity), and \(\dfrac{AL}{DM} = \dfrac{AO}{DO}\) ... (i)

The two triangles share the base BC, and AL and DM are their heights:

\(\dfrac{\text{ar}(\Delta ABC)}{\text{ar}(\Delta DBC)} = \dfrac{\frac{1}{2} \times BC \times AL}{\frac{1}{2} \times BC \times DM} = \dfrac{AL}{DM} = \dfrac{AO}{DO}\), using (i).

rows.subtopic: Surface Area of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: A wooden article was made by scooping out a hemisphere from each end of a solid cylinder, as shown in the figure. If the height of the cylinder is 10 cm and its base is of radius 3.5 cm, find the total surface area of the article.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - a shaded cylinder with a hemispherical hollow drawn at each end; every value is in the stem. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
Height of the cylinder \(h = 10\) cm, and the radius of the cylinder = radius of each hemisphere \(= r = 3.5 = \dfrac{7}{2}\) cm.

The two flat ends are scooped out, so the article is bounded by the curved surface of the cylinder and the curved surfaces of the two hemispherical hollows.

Total surface area \(=\) CSA of the cylinder \(+\) CSA of 2 hemispheres

\(= 2\pi rh + 2 \times 2\pi r^2 = 2\pi r(h + 2r)\)

\(= 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times \dfrac{7}{2}\left(10 + 2 \times \dfrac{7}{2}\right) = 22 \times 17 = 374\) cm\(^2\).
